deck.title: Benchmarking and Gap Analysis Concept Cards

cards.backDefinition: A reference level or comparison point used to judge the relative performance of a process, program, organization, or result.
cards.whyItMatters: A benchmark gives performance data context, helping an organization see whether current results are weak, typical, strong, or in need of improvement.
cards.keyPoint: A benchmark is the reference point; benchmarking is the comparison process.

sourceRefs.locator: Action item 1 > compare results to similar facilities or other employers

cards.backDefinition: A structured process of comparing performance, practices, or results with relevant internal units, competitors, industry references, benchmarks, or leading performers.
cards.whyItMatters: Benchmarking can reveal challenge areas and improvement opportunities that are difficult to see when an organization reviews only its own historical results.
cards.keyPoint: Choose comparison sources that are relevant enough to support useful decisions.

cards.backDefinition: A defined quantitative or qualitative measure used to track performance, progress, implementation, or results over time.
cards.whyItMatters: Well-chosen measures turn broad goals into observable evidence that can be reviewed, compared, and used for decisions.
cards.keyPoint: A useful measure should be relevant, accurate, timely, and decision-oriented.

sourceRefs.locator: Measures should show trends, be accurate and timely, and support decision making
Action item 1 > define indicators and collect, analyze, and review performance data

cards.backDefinition: An established starting or current performance level used as a reference for evaluating later change, trends, or improvement.
cards.whyItMatters: Without a clear starting reference, an organization may know its current result but cannot reliably show how much performance has changed.
cards.keyPoint: A baseline anchors future comparison to a known starting level.

cards.backDefinition: A defined desired performance level used to evaluate whether a program, process, or improvement effort is progressing toward its goal.
cards.whyItMatters: Targets convert broad intentions into measurable expectations and make it easier to recognize progress, shortfalls, and the need for action.
cards.keyPoint: Track progress toward targets using relevant performance indicators.

sourceRefs.locator: Program evaluation > establishing, reporting, and tracking goals and targets

cards.backDefinition: The difference between current performance and a desired, benchmark, expected, or required level of performance.
cards.whyItMatters: Defining the gap makes the improvement need visible and helps focus attention on the size and nature of the shortfall.
cards.keyPoint: A gap describes the difference; gap analysis investigates what that difference means and what should change.

sourceRefs.locator: Assessment identifies strengths and gaps and supports cycles of improvement

cards.backDefinition: A structured comparison of current performance or practices with a desired benchmark, target, standard, or future state to identify shortcomings and improvement needs.
cards.whyItMatters: Gap analysis turns comparison findings into a clearer picture of what is missing, weak, or misaligned before resources are committed to improvement.
cards.keyPoint: Define the current state, comparison state, identified gaps, and actions needed to close them.

sourceRefs.locator: Safety and Health Program Self-Evaluation and Program Audit Tool

cards.backDefinition: Performance information from relevant internal units, competitors, industry averages, benchmarks, or leading performers used to place an organization's results in context.
cards.whyItMatters: Comparative data helps distinguish genuine strong performance from results that only appear strong when viewed without an external or internal reference.
cards.keyPoint: Select comparison data that are relevant to the decision and performance question.
